entity.name: Thales of Miletus
entity.description: The first philosopher in Western history, who replaced gods with reason. Thales proposed that water was the fundamental substance of all matter, predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BC, and calculated the height of Egypt's pyramids using shadows. Named the first of the Seven Sages of Greece, he told his mother it was always either too early or too late to marry.

story.name: Thales of Miletus
story.description: A predicted eclipse that stops a war, pyramid heights calculated by shadows, a theory that everything is water, and diplomatic counsel that saves a city. The birth of Western philosophy.

moments.name: Thales Is Born in Miletus, the Wealthiest Greek City in Ionia
moments.subtitle: A merchant port on the Turkish coast produces Western civilization's first philosopher
moments.description: Around 625 BC, Thales was born in Miletus, a prosperous mercantile city at the mouth of the Maeander River in Ionia (near modern Didim, Turkey). Ancient sources disagree on his ancestry: Herodotus described him as Phoenician by remote descent, while most writers considered him a native Milesian of distinguished family. Miletus was one of the wealthiest Greek cities of the archaic period, with trade connections spanning Egypt and Babylonia. This cosmopolitan environment, where Greek, Phoenician, and Mesopotamian knowledge intersected, provided the intellectual foundation for Thales to become what Aristotle later called the first natural philosopher.

moments.name: Thales Predicts a Solar Eclipse That Halts a War Between the Lydians and Medes
moments.subtitle: The first recorded scientific prediction in Western history stops a battle mid-fight
moments.description: On May 28, 585 BC, a solar eclipse occurred during a battle between the Lydians and the Medes near the Halys River in Anatolia. According to the historian Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, the Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus had predicted this eclipse in advance. The sudden darkness so alarmed both armies that they ceased fighting and negotiated peace. Whether Thales used Babylonian astronomical records or developed his own methods remains debated, but this is considered the earliest recorded successful scientific prediction in Western history. The date of the eclipse is one of the few firm anchors for establishing Thales's chronology.

moments.name: Thales Is Named the First of the Seven Sages of Greece
moments.subtitle: A philosopher wins a golden tripod twice and dedicates it to Apollo at Delphi
moments.description: Around 582 BC, during the archonship of Damasius at Athens, the tradition of the Seven Sages of Greece was established, and Thales was recognized as the first among them. While the other sages were primarily law-givers and statesmen, Plutarch noted that Thales alone carried his speculations beyond the practical realm. According to Diogenes Laertius, a golden tripod meant for the wisest man was passed among all seven sages and returned to Thales twice, who ultimately dedicated it to Apollo at the temple of Didyma. The maxim attributed to Thales at Delphi was "gnothi seauton" -- know thyself -- arguably the most famous philosophical motto in Western history.

moments.name: Thales Calculates the Height of Egypt's Pyramids Using Their Shadows
moments.subtitle: A Greek merchant applies geometry to solve a puzzle that stumped the Egyptians themselves
moments.description: According to multiple ancient sources, Thales of Miletus visited Egypt and calculated the height of the Great Pyramids by measuring their shadows at the moment when a person's shadow equaled their own height. This elegant application of proportional geometry -- later formalized as the intercept theorem (also called Thales's theorem) -- demonstrated a fundamentally new approach to understanding the physical world through mathematical reasoning rather than mythology. Whether Thales actually traveled to Egypt or learned from accounts of others remains disputed, but Miletus maintained a permanent colony at Naucratis in Egypt, making the visit plausible. The method itself became a foundational example of applied mathematics.

moments.name: Thales Advises Miletus to Stay Neutral, Saving the City from Persian Conquest
moments.subtitle: The philosopher's diplomatic counsel spares his city when Cyrus the Great destroys Lydia
moments.description: Around 546 BC, Thales gained fame as a political counselor when he advised the Milesians not to enter a military alliance with the Lydians against Cyrus the Great of Persia. When Cyrus defeated King Croesus and conquered Sardis, the Lydian capital, Miletus was spared because it had taken no hostile action. The other eleven cities of the Ionian League, which had not heeded such counsel, were subjugated by the Persians. Thales further proposed that the Ionian cities establish a single seat of government at Teos, the geographic center of Ionia, while maintaining local autonomy -- an early concept of federal governance that went unheeded.
